title: Randomized sampling & quick rubric (scratch)
content:
Purpose:
Quick, ad-hoc working notes for a randomized sampling approach I used to hunt subtle regressions in generation quality. This is a scratchpad — half heuristics, half hypotheses and quick examples. Meant to be low-effort reproducible checks that I can run during nights or while triaging a flaky rollout.

Problem context:
- Observed small uptick in user complaints about hallucinated citations for the news summarization route (hosted-api, model variant: open-7b-qlora).
- Regression only shows up on ~0.6% of sampled traffic, often when prompts include multiple source bullets and a soft instruction to "cite sources".

Goals for this doc:
1) Define a compact rubric I can apply quickly to a randomized sample.
2) Capture concrete prompt/output pairs that illustrate failure modes.
3) Note quick hypotheses and next steps for lightweight fixes / experiments.

Sampling approach (randomized, stratified-ish):
- Pull 1k responses from production route over 24h, stratify by token length buckets: short (<60), medium (60-220), long (>220).
- Keep only items with user instruction containing words: cite/citation/sources/reference.
- From each bucket, take random 50 samples for human review (~150 total).
- For fast triage, annotate with 3-shot quick rubric below.

Quick rubric (0-3, single integer):
- 3 = Good — answer cites credible/explicit sources or correctly says "no sources available". No hallucination.
- 2 = Mostly OK — provides reasonable paraphrase but source attribution vague (e.g., "according to reports"). Not ideal but acceptable.
- 1 = Concerning — fabricates specific source names, dates, or URLs that are verifiably wrong.
- 0 = Bad — confidently invents multiple precise citations (authors, publication names) that don't exist or are clearly incorrect.

Rubric examples (toy):
- Prompt: "Summarize the two main policy steps and cite sources."
  Model output A (score 3): "According to NY Times (Aug 2025) and Reuters (Aug 2025)..." [both links provided and verifiable] -> 3
  Model output B (score 1): "Reported by The Beacon Daily (July 2024) and Dr. L. Kerr in Policy Review" [no such articles] -> 1

Observed failure modes in current sample:
- Mode 1: Confident micro-hallucinations (fabricated article titles) when the answer includes a short list of facts + source list. Often triggered when prompt contains bullet list of claims.
- Mode 2: Source drift — model cites outdated or wrong dates (e.g., citing a 2022 study for a 2024 claim) — probably prompt/recency mismatch.
- Mode 3: Overuse of generic "news outlets" phrasing (vague attribution) that reduces user trust but isn't technically false.

Counts from quick pass (n=150):
- Score 3: 92
- Score 2: 33
- Score 1: 17
- Score 0: 8
Notes: non-trivial fraction of 1/0 are concentrated in the long token bucket (>220).

Mini hypotheses:
- H1: The model's citation behavior is sensitive to prompt framing (explicit "list sources with links" vs. "cite sources").
- H2: Long inputs push the model to synthesize placeholders when retrieval context is missing — maybe KV cache truncation or late-context attention change.
- H3: A quantization/compilation kernel change (recent release) slightly changed the decoding distribution on long sequences leading to more confident low-prob hallucinations.

Quick experiments to run (priority order):
- E1: Prompt perturbation A/B: compare explicit template ("List each claim and include a source URL if available. If none, say 'no primary source' ") vs baseline. Sample 200 each. (Owner: me)
- E2: Short-prefix cache test: run same samples on variant with extended KV cache retention (dedicated test cluster). See if long-bucket regressions drop. (Owner: infra: @Ethan Park)
- E3: Rollback candidate: test small inference engine kernel change from release X vs X-1 on small held-out set. (Linked to JIRA INF-4921). (Owner: eng-runtime)

Annotation protocol notes (how I scored):
- If model names a specific article + date + author, I quickly try to google the tuple — if nothing shows and multiple quick checks fail, mark 1 or 0 depending on number of fabrications.
- When output includes a generic outlet with plausible-sounding headline but no link, mark 2 and add a comment.
- I keep a short "evidence" note: whether a web search returned match, and which terms I used.

Representative samples (copied raw):
- Prompt 1: "Summarize and cite sources for these bullets: - new export control - tech investment guidelines - public response"
  Model: "According to The Pacific Ledger (Jan 2025), ..."  // web search returned nothing, similar names exist but no article -> score 1. Comment: "Pacific Ledger likely hallucinated; try exact match terms."

- Prompt 2: "Short summary + sources" (long context ~380 tokens)
  Model: lists three sources with plausible URLs but all redirect to redwood-inference.com (odd). -> score 0. Comment: "URL reuse / placeholder bug? look at post-processing pipeline that rewrites urls."

Open questions / things I'm unsure about:
- Is there a post-processing pass that canonicalizes source names/URLs (this could explain URL reuse)? Need to confirm with infra.
- Could the model catalog change mention (open-7b-qlora v2) coincide with kernel change impacting sampling temperature? Cross-check release dates.

Quick todo (actionable):
- [ ] Run prompt-perturbation experiment (E1) — script in github evals PR #742 (I will fork and add a 200-run test).
- [ ] Ping infra about KV cache retention test (E2) — @Ethan Park in Slack.
- [ ] Add 20 more long-bucket samples to see distribution robustness.
- [ ] Attach top 5 worst 0/1 outputs to JIRA INF-4921 as examples.

Notes to self: keep annotations lightweight — aim for ~90s per sample. If something looks systemic, escalate and attach examples. Save this file as living doc; will prune once we have E1/E2 results.

Related links:
- Quick search terms I used for verification: article title (in quotes) + author + site (site:news), sometimes with "pdf" appended for policy docs.
- Slack thread: slack://thread/C8J4Q12AA-163820 (contains two user screenshots).

End of scratchpad.

-- Samira K.
